records.d: Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier on October 14, 1947, in the Bell X-1: the first supersonic flight. The barrier was psychological. Speed had a new limit.
records.h: The rocket-powered X-1 exceeded Mach 1 in level flight, proving controlled supersonic flight possible. The data was military. The barrier fell.
records.mj: Established - documented October 14, 1947 flight; first supersonic flight.

records.d: Britain and France signed the Concorde treaty in 1962: a supersonic airliner as a joint project. The race to fly passengers supersonically began. The treaty was the starting gun.
records.h: The agreement launched development of a Mach 2 airliner. The partnership was political and technical. The race was on.
records.mj: Established - documented 1962 treaty; Anglo-French supersonic airliner project.
records.z: timeline|year=1962|span=1|events=Concorde treaty signed~supersonic airliner race begins

records.d: The Soviet Tu-144 first flew on December 31, 1968: the first supersonic airliner to fly. The race had two runners. The Cold War went Mach 2.
records.h: The delta-wing airliner beat Concorde to first flight by two months. The competition was geopolitical. The technology was parallel.
records.mj: Established - documented December 31, 1968 flight; first supersonic airliner.

records.d: Concorde first flew on March 2, 1969: the Anglo-French challenger. The elegant delta took wing. The icon was born.
records.h: The slender delta flew from Toulouse, beginning a long test program. The design was refined. The icon flew.
records.mj: Established - documented March 2, 1969 flight; Concorde first flight.

records.d: The FAA banned civil supersonic flight over land in 1973: the sonic boom limited supersonics to oceans. The boom was the law. Speed had a geography.
records.h: The rule prohibited Mach 1+ over US land due to boom annoyance. The market shrank to transatlantic. The geography was legal.
records.mj: Established - documented 1973 FAA rule; overland supersonic ban.

records.d: Concorde entered service on January 21, 1976: passengers flying at Mach 2. The supersonic age began. Lunch in London, dinner in New York, faster.
records.h: British Airways and Air France flew scheduled Mach 2 service across the Atlantic. The flight was 3.5 hours. The age was exclusive.
records.mj: Established - documented January 21, 1976 service entry; scheduled supersonic flights.

records.d: The Tu-144 began passenger service in November 1977: the Soviet supersonic airliner flew fare-paying passengers. The race had a second airline. The service was brief.
records.h: Aeroflot flew limited supersonic passenger routes. The operations were troubled. The service lasted months.
records.mj: Established - documented November 1977 service; Tu-144 passenger flights.

records.d: Tu-144 passenger service ended in 1978 after a crash: the Soviet supersonic dream grounded. The race lost a runner. One supersonic airliner remained.
records.h: A test-flight crash ended passenger operations. The program continued as testbed. The dream was grounded.
records.mj: Established - documented 1978 end; Tu-144 passenger service ended.

records.d: Air France Flight 4590 crashed on July 25, 2000: Concorde's only fatal accident. The perfect safety record broke. The icon was wounded.
records.h: Debris on the runway caused a tire burst and fuel fire. The BEA investigation was thorough. The grounding followed.
records.mj: Established - documented July 25, 2000 crash; BEA investigation.

records.d: Concorde retired in October 2003: the supersonic age ended. The sky went subsonic. The dream waited.
records.h: Rising costs and falling demand ended scheduled Mach 2 service. The farewell flights were emotional. The age closed.
records.mj: Established - documented October 2003 retirement; end of Concorde service.

records.d: Boom Supersonic was founded in 2014: the startup to return supersonic travel. The garage met Mach 2. The comeback began.
records.h: The company pursued a commercial supersonic airliner with modern economics. The bet was technology. The comeback was funded.
records.mj: Established - documented 2014 founding; Boom Supersonic.

records.d: NASA's X-59 low-boom demonstrator program advanced in 2017-2018: the quiet supersonic. The boom would become a thump. The ban's solution flew.
records.h: Lockheed Martin built the X-plane to demonstrate low-boom flight for regulators. The data would inform rules. The thump was the goal.
records.mj: Established - documented NASA X-59 program; low-boom flight demonstrator.

records.d: Boom rolled out the XB-1 demonstrator in October 2020: the baby Boom. The supersonic demonstrator was real. The test program began.
records.h: The one-third-scale demonstrator would prove the aerodynamics. The rollout was virtual. The program was serious.
records.mj: Established - documented October 2020 rollout; XB-1 demonstrator.

records.d: United ordered 15 Boom Overtures in June 2021: the airline bet on supersonic. The order book opened. Demand was real.
records.h: The conditional order for 15 aircraft with options validated the market. The bet was corporate. The book was open.
records.mj: Established - documented June 2021 order; United Boom Overture order.

records.d: Aerion shut down in May 2021: the supersonic business jet dream ended. Capital intensity won. The field narrowed.
records.h: Funding shortfalls ended the AS2 program. The lesson was cost. The race had fewer runners.
records.mj: Established - documented May 2021 shutdown; Aerion closure.

records.d: American Airlines ordered 20 Overtures in August 2022: the second airline bet. The order book grew. The market doubled down.
records.h: The conditional order expanded Boom's backlog. The confidence was industry-wide. The book grew.
records.mj: Established - documented August 2022 order; American Airlines Overture order.

records.d: Boom announced the Symphony engine in December 2022: a custom supersonic powerplant. The engine would be bespoke. The supply chain was vertical.
records.h: The clean-sheet engine design targeted Overture's needs. The integration was tight. The powerplant was owned.
records.mj: Established - documented December 2022 announcement; Symphony engine.

records.d: The XB-1 first flew on March 22, 2024: the demonstrator flew. The comeback had wings. The test program was airborne.
records.h: The flight from Mojave validated the aerodynamics. The program advanced. The wings worked.
records.mj: Established - documented March 22, 2024 flight; XB-1 first flight.

records.d: NASA rolled out the X-59 in January 2024: the quiet supersonic X-plane revealed. The thump had a shape. The data campaign began.
records.h: The long-nosed demonstrator was unveiled at Lockheed's Skunk Works. The flights would follow. The shape was the experiment.
records.mj: Established - documented January 2024 rollout; X-59 unveiled.

records.d: The XB-1 broke the sound barrier on January 28, 2025: the first civil supersonic flight in decades. The barrier fell again. The comeback was real.
records.h: The demonstrator exceeded Mach 1 in test flight. The milestone was historic. The return was proven.
records.mj: Established - documented January 28, 2025 flight; XB-1 supersonic.

records.d: By 2025, low-boom flight tests were advancing: the thump measured over communities. The data accumulated. The ban's evidence grew.
records.h: X-59 community overflights would measure public response to low booms. The science was acoustic. The evidence was the point.
records.mj: Emerging - real program; X-59 low-boom community testing.

records.d: By 2025, regulators were reviewing the overland supersonic ban: low-boom data informing new rules. The 1973 law faced science. The geography might change.
records.h: FAA and international bodies studied noise-based standards to replace the Mach cutoff. The rule would become acoustic. The map might open.
records.mj: Emerging - real regulatory process; overland supersonic rule review.
